title: The Encirclement Closes
subtitle: The German junction and the Soviet struggle to reopen a route
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: German mobile forces joined east of Kiev during 15–16 September. Soviet relief attacks and movements inside the pocket tested a perimeter that the Germans still had to consolidate.
body:
A junction that had to be held

By 16 September 1941, German mobile forces advancing from north and south had joined east of Kiev. The main body of the Soviet Southwestern Front had lost an unobstructed route to the Soviet interior. The Germans still had to hold their junction against men trying to escape and forces attempting to break in. Infantry had to catch up; exhausted mobile formations had to guard crossings and roads. Closure changed what a Soviet withdrawal required. It would now take an attack to open the route, followed by enough time to move more than the first troops through it. [1]

The warning examined in The Kiev Trap had become a barrier behind the Soviet armies. It consisted of defended roads, bridges and settlements, with stronger and weaker intervals between them. The Germans had to resist escape attempts from the west and relief attacks from the east. Soviet commanders had to find a usable passage through that changing network before their own communications and organisation broke down.

The main pocket contained the 5th, 21st, 26th and 37th Armies, front headquarters and supporting organisations, though an army’s name does not place all its personnel on one side of the barrier. The 38th and 40th continued fighting outside while losing contact with some of their formations; other armies also had units separated by the German advance. The front was being divided through its working connections, rather than moved intact into one enclosure.[1][2]a

Reading the linkup carefully

The northern spearhead came from Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group, especially the 3rd Panzer Division, while Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group approached from the Kremenchuk bridgehead. Robert Kirchubel identifies contact between elements of the 3rd and Hans-Valentin Hube’s 16th Panzer Divisions around Lokhvytsia on 15 September. His notes acknowledge alternative dating. Guderian’s retrospective account places a further contact by the 3rd Panzer Division’s advance battalion on 16 September along the Udai north of Lubny. These accounts establish the convergence during 15–16 September; they do not justify assigning every contact to one location and one exact hour.[3][4]

Contact between patrols, a junction that could be maintained and a consolidated perimeter were separate achievements. Their timing may account for some differences between Kirchubel and Guderian, but the cited accounts do not settle the exact sequence of first contact. What can be established is the convergence on 15–16 September and its consequence by this study’s date: the principal Soviet grouping lay west of a German barrier. An exact first-contact minute would give the evidence a precision it does not possess.

Geography explains why Lokhvytsia and Lubny both appear in the story. The mobile columns were operating across a zone containing several rivers and road junctions, rather than along two straight arrows ending at one point. A detachment could make contact near one town while another secured a crossing farther south. The Udai and Sula systems created obstacles that could protect a German position or obstruct a Soviet escape. Controlling a bridge had particular value because vehicles, guns and horse-drawn columns could not pass through the countryside as freely as small groups on foot. Closure therefore developed through control of communications as much as through occupation of a continuous front.

Guderian’s account records the 4th Panzer Division reaching the Udai and other formations moving into positions that tightened the enclosure. It also describes the transfer of responsibility along the line as units from Kleist’s group relieved parts of the northern force. Such relief was essential. A spearhead sent to make contact had to retain enough freedom to meet a counterattack or move towards another threatened crossing. Leaving every mobile unit fixed at its furthest point would sacrifice the ability to respond elsewhere. The German operation consequently required a second sequence of movements after the dramatic first junction.[4]b

The telephone line across the junction

In his retrospective account, Guderian credited Colonel Albert Praun with establishing a telephone connection from Romny to Kleist’s group through Lokhvytsia and Lubny. The account presents an achievement of Guderian’s command, but the practical problem was shared by both forces. Forward troops could meet before their headquarters had a dependable way to coordinate artillery, reserves or relief. Laying and maintaining the line helped turn contact between detachments into cooperation between larger formations. Without it, officers behind the junction might still be unsure what their neighbours were doing.[4]c

Reinforcements arriving inside the danger

The Soviet effort to block the German movement had continued while the junction was forming. The 289th Rifle Division was being sent towards Pyriatyn, and the 7th Motorised Rifle Division towards Pryluky. A report for the evening of 13 September recorded four trains of the 289th already in the Pyriatyn area, another approaching, two loading at Zolotonosha and rolling stock provided for two more. This is a particularly useful description because it shows the division distributed across the transport system. It had been assigned a task, but it did not yet exist at its destination as a complete force ready to execute it.[2]

For the 7th Motorised Rifle Division, the front specified two road routes through the area east of Kiev towards Pryluky, with a deadline for concentration on 13 September. Air cover was requested, and reports were required as each movement departed and arrived. These provisions reveal the headquarters’ concern with the interval between an order and its implementation. Splitting the movement between roads could reduce congestion but also made coordination more demanding. A delay at one crossing might leave one part of the division arriving while another remained far behind. The order demonstrates intended movement; it does not prove that every column met the schedule.[2]

At Pyriatyn, the 289th Division was instructed to defend approaches from the east and southeast. Antiaircraft guns and machine-gun units were subordinated to it for ground defence. The direction of that assignment shows how radically the front had changed: forces in what had been the rear now had to face the enemy coming towards them from the interior side of the Soviet position. A subsequent order emphasised the roads to Pyriatyn and Hrebinka and the need for contact with the Lubny garrison. The objective was to preserve a connected defensive space rather than protect one town in isolation.[2]d

Meanwhile, the older army fronts were losing coherence. The 13 September summary described the 5th Army’s units as small, poorly organised and equipped predominantly with rifles. Other reports recorded formations fighting in local encirclements and emerging in separate groups. These were not all parts of one synchronised retreat. Some troops were still resisting attacks from the west or north while German mobile forces were already behind them. A commander trying to reorganise those survivors had to establish where they were, identify what weapons they retained and place them under authority before they could contribute to a larger breakout.[2]

The front continued to order limited attacks intended to reconnect neighbouring armies. On 14 September the 5th and 37th Armies were directed to strike towards Kobyzhcha and restore contact between their flanks. Their main forces were still expected to hold their existing positions. These orders sought to repair an internal rupture, but the wider encirclement was forming farther east. A local success could improve communications without opening the route to safety. This was one of the central difficulties of the Soviet response: the front had several gaps, and closing one did not necessarily address the gap that determined whether the entire grouping could escape.[2]e

The struggle outside the ring

Soviet forces outside the pocket were intended to strike the German eastern flank. On the night of 14 September, Timoshenko ordered Pavel Belov to form a cavalry-mechanised group from the 2nd Cavalry Corps, the 1st and 129th Tank Brigades and the 100th Rifle Division. It was to attack towards Romny on 16 September and restore the connection between the 40th and 21st Armies. The directive noted that the 1st Tank Brigade and 100th Division would begin arriving at their railway stations on 15 September. The timetable again compressed arrival, assembly and combat into an exceptionally short interval.[2]

Belov’s cavalry could move mounted and fight on foot, combining its mobility with artillery and attached tanks. The brigades were meant to add striking power, but horses needed fodder while tanks needed fuel, and formations with different marching speeds still needed to meet at the right time. A mixed group could use some routes unsuitable for a fully motorised force without escaping the need for supplies, communications and coordinated movement.

A second effort involved the 5th Cavalry Corps and tank brigades farther south. On 15 September, theatre headquarters described attacks towards Khorol and Romny as related measures against the two German penetrations. By the evening of 16 September, its directive also required defence of the Psel crossings and the Poltava approaches. The tasks were widening: relief of the threatened front had to be combined with prevention of further German movement east. The force outside the encirclement could not devote every available unit to breaking inward because it was also becoming the defence of the territory beyond the pocket.[2]

These attacks did not rescue the encircled armies, but they were not imaginary. On 17 September, Timoshenko reported Belov’s main forces moving through the Olshana–Berestovka line towards Romny. Guderian’s account describes a serious attack against Romny on 18 September that forced him to collect local reserves, including infantry, antiaircraft guns and tanks. The two records do not allow every Soviet column to be matched to a German report, but together they establish that the eastern side of the German operation remained contested. The encircling forces had to defend against troops approaching from outside as well as those trying to escape.[2][4]f

This is the distinction between an inner and an outer encirclement front. The inner front faces the trapped forces and tries to prevent their departure. The outer front faces relief attacks and protects the encircling troops’ own communications. If the outer front gives way, an inward-facing formation may find itself attacked from behind. If too many troops are shifted outward, the trapped enemy may break through the weakened inner line. German operational success depended on managing both demands, and the arrival of infantry could be as important as another tank advance because it allowed mobile forces to respond where pressure was greatest.

The direction of Soviet headquarters movement reflected this widening emergency. At 22.00 on 16 September, Timoshenko’s military council left for Akhtyrka to direct the fighting towards Romny, while a command post for the main theatre headquarters was being prepared near Kharkov. These were not movements of the encircled front headquarters itself. Distinguishing them matters because several levels of command were now separated geographically, each receiving a different view of the battle. Moving senior officers nearer the relief operation could improve their contact with those forces while increasing their dependence on communications for events elsewhere. Headquarters mobility offered a partial remedy for distance, but it could not make distance disappear.[2]

The Psel line shows how relief and defence could pull in different directions. Orders to the 5th Cavalry Corps combined preventing German crossings with active operations west of the river. The 38th Army was required to halt its retreat, defend the eastern bank and retain reserves near Poltava. Engineers were included in the assigned group because a river defence needed preparation as well as troops. These instructions sought to prevent the Kiev disaster from becoming a still wider collapse towards the east. For the trapped armies, however, every formation held to protect a crossing or town outside the pocket was a formation whose contribution to relief was constrained by another responsibility.[2]g

Orders, permission and the loss of time

On 16 September, Timoshenko continued to demand attacks towards Romny and Lubny. He called for a northern group of two or three divisions with artillery, criticised what he termed passive resistance, and permitted some Kiev defenders to be used near Kozelets. The intention was to defeat the enclosing forces without abandoning the wider position. The depleted units and damaged communications described in front reports made assembling that group increasingly difficult.[2]

The formal Stavka authorisation to leave Kiev came later. Directive 002087, timed at 23.40 on 17 September, permitted abandonment of the fortified region and city and withdrawal to the eastern bank of the Dnieper under the front commander’s arrangements. It ordered weapons removed where possible and destroyed where evacuation was impossible, together with the bridges and other military installations. Its wording is narrower than a general instruction to withdraw the whole front to safety beyond the German pincers. The permission removed the obligation to retain the city, but it did not remove the enemy barrier farther east.[2]

The distinction is consequential. Troops west of the Dnieper first had to reach and cross the river; troops already east of it still had to move through the larger encirclement. Destroying bridges after withdrawal could delay German pursuit, but destroying them before every intended unit had crossed could trap additional men. Heavy weapons presented another choice between preserving fighting power and maintaining movement. The directive established priorities, but execution required local information that was increasingly difficult to obtain. A successful crossing by one group could coexist with the loss of another whose orders arrived late or whose route had already been cut.

The 37th Army’s own message, relayed on 17 September, described exhausted units, depleted reserves and broken contact with neighbours. It warned of threats to the Kiev crossings from the east and of large accumulations of transport in Kiev and Darnytsia. These details show why the permission to move did not produce an orderly evacuation. Vehicles and people were already concentrated near the very points through which withdrawal had to pass. The army could still resist, but it lacked the reserves and clear communications needed to control every approach while moving its main body.[2]

By 18 September, reports reaching theatre headquarters indicated that Kirponos’s command was organising an eastward attack. That is the appropriate description of the changed operation. The troops were no longer simply withdrawing along an open route; they were seeking to force a way through hostile positions. The difference affected ammunition expenditure, the employment of artillery and the sequence in which columns could move. A formation assigned to lead had to fight while those behind it waited, consuming supplies and remaining exposed to attacks elsewhere. Success required both making a gap and keeping it open long enough for more than the leading troops to pass.[2]h

People and institutions in a moving pocket

As the front contracted, military and civilian movements shared the same towns and roads. Pyriatyn and the Kiev crossings carried scattered units, vehicles and displaced people through places whose residents also needed food and information. Operational reports used broad collective descriptions that cannot supply an exact refugee count. They nevertheless record an army’s institutions moving through inhabited space, rather than an empty landscape reserved for military columns.

A front directive of 13 September addressed the functioning of rear services directly. It ordered army military councils to take personal responsibility for organisation, keep institutions within their assigned boundaries and arrange protection against attacks from the air and ground. It also called for harsh measures to restore order. The wording shows the coercive response to dislocation, but it does not by itself identify particular punishments carried out. The underlying problem was that a medical unit, depot or transport office displaced from its normal position could cease serving the troops that depended on it, even if its personnel and stores survived.[2]i

Medical evacuation was especially vulnerable to this disruption. A wounded soldier needed more than an opening in the German line: he needed someone able to move him, a vehicle or cart where necessary and a destination at which care could continue. Transport assigned to casualties could not simultaneously carry the same load of ammunition or food. Such competing uses explain why the survival of a military organisation mattered beyond its fighting strength. As headquarters lost control and columns fragmented, the people least able to move independently faced the greatest difficulty. The loss of transport therefore changed who could attempt escape, leaving the most seriously wounded dependent on assistance that fragmented formations were increasingly unable to organise.

A flight out of the pocket

Colonel Ryazanov carried news out of the pocket by aircraft on 18 September. Pokrovsky relayed his account: German troops had reached points around Pyriatyn, the town was crowded, and nearby ground had reportedly been under mortar fire when he left at four in the morning. The report retained uncertainties about locations and the changing situation. One officer’s journey briefly restored a connection that ordinary communications no longer maintained. It brought recent observations to higher headquarters without providing a complete picture of the pocket.[2]j

The encirclement was being completed while mass murder continued in areas occupied earlier. On 15 September, SS and police personnel, assisted by Ukrainian municipal police, murdered approximately 12,000 Jews near the airfield at Berdichev, now Berdychiv, according to the Foundation Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe. The city had been occupied in July; a ghetto was established on 26 August, and successive shootings preceded the September massacre. A minority of workers were temporarily spared. The dated sequence matters: persecution developed through confinement, forced labour and organised killing, rather than beginning only when a nearby military operation ended. It also links the expanding role of Jeckeln’s police apparatus to the later murder of Kiev’s Jews. These crimes were perpetrated against communities already under occupation, while the armies closing the pocket were bringing more people within German power. [5]k

Within the pocket, the chance to escape depended partly on what a group could carry. Men on foot might pass through a gap that could not accommodate guns, carts or ambulances. Abandoning equipment could improve their immediate prospects while destroying the formation’s ability to fight after it emerged. Retaining it could slow them until the passage closed. This was the predicament behind the distinction between rescuing soldiers and rescuing an army. Neither outcome can be inferred simply from the other, and the men least able to move independently were especially dependent on the survival of organised transport.

Encirclement as an operation, not an ending

The German achievement was formidable because it converted two long advances into a barrier behind several Soviet armies. It was also expensive to maintain. Troops watching crossings needed ammunition and food; mobile reserves needed fuel; damaged vehicles needed recovery; infantry closing from the west needed time. German commanders could not count every soldier inside the perimeter as already captured or every road inside it as already secured. Continued Soviet attacks around Romny and elsewhere show that the operational victory still contained immediate dangers for the forces enforcing it.[4]l

For the Soviets, the change was more severe. The same tasks that an army ordinarily performs in sequence now competed within a shrinking area: establish positions, locate neighbours, obtain supplies, evacuate wounded men and prepare movement. Each failure made the others harder. Lost communication delayed concentration; delayed concentration exposed units to separate attack; separate defeats reduced the force available to open an exit. This cumulative process explains why some formations could continue to fight effectively for a time while the front as a coordinated organisation moved towards destruction.

On 16 September, the German junction had become a barrier behind the Soviet armies, while the Soviet relief effort remained unable to break it. The defenders of Kiev still had to leave the city; Kirponos’s headquarters still sought a way to coordinate escape. German victory now depended on keeping those movements fragmented long enough to destroy the trapped formations. The Fall of Kiev follows the city’s abandonment and the occupation that began while the pocket battle continued to its east.

sourceMethod: Lettered notes retain detailed references, access limits and qualifications; numbered citations lead to the sources below. Retrospective accounts, translated extracts and abstracts are identified where used. Later events retain their own dates. The dated atlas has separate feature sources and precision notes.
